data.title: Working on my own terms
data.description:
AT 76, I still look forward to having something meaningful to do each day.

My golden years give me greater freedom to choose how I spend my time, be it by contributing through work, sharing what I have learnt, serving the community or enjoying the people and pursuits that enrich my life.

Recently, my Raffles Institution cohort celebrated the 60 years since completing our O levels in 1966. Many schoolmates have retired and are enjoying travel, family life and community service.

I am among the few who continue to work. Our paths differ, but we all face a worthwhile question: How do we make these years fulfilling?

A fulfilling life need not include paid work, a board appointment or a crowded diary. It can be found in caring for family, pursuing a new hobby, joining a community group or being a dependable mentor.

What matters is that the individual remains interested in life and connected to others.

Work with a different purpose

At this stage, work is less about earning money and more about engaging my mind and putting my experience to good use.

Board discussions and advisory assignments require me to listen carefully, question assumptions and consider unfamiliar problems. They are a form of mental gymnastics I enjoy, and I hope such stimulating intellectual challenges will keep dementia at bay.

My corporate roles also connect me with people across countries, industries and generations. Experience gives me a perspective to offer, though I do not assume to have all the answers. Younger colleagues often help me see fresh possibilities.

Having spent more than 30 years as a CEO, technopreneur and private investor, including my tenure as vice-president and managing director for the Asia-Pacific at Compaq, I have helped businesses with listings, mergers, accelerated growth and turnarounds.

These experiences have value beyond the positions I once held. The lessons learnt from difficult decisions, mistakes and setbacks can help others navigate their own challenges. Our usefulness does not end when our formal careers do.

Share what experience has taught us

Teaching entrepreneurship and leadership at the National University of Singapore, alongside mentoring members of the Singapore Institute of Directors and other professional networks, have allowed me to pass on some of these lessons. Knowledge accumulated over five decades should be passed on.

Mentoring is a rewarding way for seniors to contribute, and it need not happen through a formal programme. We can help a young colleague think through a career decision or encourage someone recovering from a setback. Sometimes, attentive listening is more useful than advice.

Learning also flows both ways. Younger people bring fresh perspectives and introduce unfamiliar technologies. Seniors should remain willing to learn and ask for help.

Find fulfilment in service

Public and community service have brought me deep fulfilment.

Through my mediation work with the State Courts and community centres, I have helped people resolve disputes in business and with family and neighbours.

When parties reach a settlement, I feel privileged to have helped them find a way forward – a reminder to be grateful for the peace in my own life.

I also served as a Justice of the Peace for 15 years and continue to solemnise marriages. Helping couples begin their journey together is a joy; it gives me an opportunity to share advice drawn from my former leadership roles at the National Family Council and the Centre for Fathering.

Service is open to all of us. A senior need not chair an organisation to make a difference. Reading with a child, visiting someone who lives alone or calling a withdrawn friend can be a meaningful contribution. We can all give the gift of time.

Discover new interests

Writing has enabled me to turn reflections into something useful to others. I have authored six books – including Golden Nuggets, an anthology of stories by seniors – which have collectively raised more than S$3 million for charities.

But we do not need to publish a book to preserve our stories; recording these tales or sharing memories with grandchildren leaves a precious inheritance.

Another source of pleasure is birding, which I took up five years ago after a slipped disc led me to give up golf. It has brought me to local spots like Kranji Marshes and overseas locations in search of unfamiliar species.

My camera now accompanies me on business trips to cities from London to Shanghai, and I go birding whenever time permits.

Birding has taught me to slow down and enjoy discovery. For other seniors, that delight may come from painting, cooking or learning about artificial intelligence.

We are never obliged to remain the people our careers required us to be.

Plan for the next chapter

Staying active requires judgment. Health, mobility and finances differ. During illness or recovery, participation may take a quieter form: a telephone conversation, reading or light activity with a friend.

Accepting help can make continued engagement possible.

We must also be willing to let go of roles that no longer fit. Saying “yes” to purpose sometimes requires saying “no” to more activity, ensuring we make time for relationships that are central to the lives we enjoy. Making time for my wife, children, children-in-law and grandchildren is as worthwhile as any professional achievement.

Earlier as an engineering student, I developed a life plan with three stages.

In Plan A, I would work for others and for money. In my current Plan B, I let others and money work for me, giving me greater freedom to choose my contributions.

In Plan C, which I intend to move towards at 80, I hope to devote more time to two areas spelled with a capital “C” – Church and Charity – and less to the smaller “c” – corporate commitments – while retaining selected engagements where I can be useful.

Crucially, the plan can evolve. Its value is that it encourages me to think deliberately about how I want to live.

The average lifespan of a Singaporean man is 84 years. Theoretically, I have eight more years to live, but that is not a given. I prefer to treat that uncertainty as a reason to appreciate today.

For seniors wondering where to begin, choose one manageable step: contact a friend, explore a hobby, learn something unfamiliar or offer an hour of help. Each is a reason to look forward to tomorrow.

I share my journey to encourage active, joyful ageing. There is still much to enjoy, discover and contribute. “No time” should never be an excuse to pursue a worthwhile purpose.

If I can have a vertical take-off from the short runway ahead of me, I will seize it to enjoy my life to the fullest.

For these reasons, retirement is not in my vocabulary.

The writer is the former vice-president and managing director of Compaq Computer Asia-Pacific. He is also a board member, senior advisor, adjunct professor and mediator.

Switching Lanes is a column exploring the diverse realities of life after a full-time career. From finding fresh purpose to savouring newfound freedom, we are redefining retirement.

Have a perspective to share? Write to btletter@sph.com.sg with the subject, Switching Lanes.

data.title: US lawmakers near deal to ban Chinese cars, spare Mercedes
data.description:
[WASHINGTON] Lawmakers in Washington are closing in on a deal to ban Chinese cars from the US, said people familiar with the matter, following last-minute negotiations aimed in part at sparing Mercedes-Benz, which is nearly 20 per cent owned by Chinese entities.

Republicans and Democrats from car-producing states behind the effort aim to send a bill to President Donald Trump’s desk by the end of the year, said the people, who asked not to be identified because the deliberations are private.

If enacted, the profitable US car market would be walled off to automakers such as BYD and Geely Automobile, whose low-cost, technology-packed electric vehicles have rapidly gained market share in Europe and South America.

Chinese cars are effectively shut out of the US because of steep tariffs and restrictions on Chinese vehicle technology imposed by the Commerce Department.

Enshrining a ban into law would take those measures a step further to address growing concerns about national and economic security threats posed by China’s ambition to dominate the global car industry.

Details about the measure are still being hammered out.

Republican Senator Bernie Moreno on Wednesday (Nov 18) briefed automaker representatives on changes under consideration to earlier legislation that aimed to block Chinese connected vehicles from the US, including provisions that would shield Mercedes from an outright ban, said the people.

Automaker representatives were broadly supportive of the effort Moreno described, though a Mercedes official voiced reservations and negotiations remain under way, the people said.

Proponents are working to pass the measure before the next Congress begins in January.

“We continue to meet with all stakeholders who have a shared interest in ensuring this important legislation becomes law in this Congress,” Mercedes said.

Agreement as early as this week

A bill advanced by a Senate panel earlier this year would have prohibited manufacturers that are more than 15 per cent owned by Chinese entities from selling cars equipped with technology that can transmit data.

Mercedes, which has lobbied for changes to that bill, is nearly 10 per cent owned by China’s BAIC Motor, a state-owned carmaker.

Li Shu Fu, the billionaire founder of Chinese carmaker Geely, also holds nearly 10 per cent of Mercedes’ shares, putting the company above the earlier bill’s 15 per cent threshold.

Lawmakers are in talks with multiple parties, including Mercedes, and have expressed optimism that an agreement could be reached as early as this week, said one person close to the talks who asked not to be identified.

Provisions under discussion include looser rules for companies with passive ownership stakes that lack voting power and how such an approach would be structured and verified.

The White House did not respond to requests for comment.

Republican Senator Katie Britt of Alabama, a major hub of Mercedes’ sport utility vehicle production, said she has worked through the bill with Moreno and believes both Mercedes and Alabama will be protected.

“We understand that there will be some adjustments that have to be made, but feel good about Mercedes continuing to be able to thrive in our state and across the country,” she said.

Banning Chinese cars would also run counter to a more permissive approach taken by Europe and Canada. Chinese automakers have quickly made inroads in Europe, in particular, leading to intense competition with home-grown brands.

The EU has started to pull back after Chinese automakers rapidly expanded their share of the market there, reaching an agreement last month with China to curb imports of hybrid vehicles into the bloc. BLOOMBERG

data.title: PM Wong and Xi pledge to deepen Singapore-China ties amid major global shake-ups
data.description:
[SHENZHEN] Singapore and China enjoy a longstanding friendship and close partnership that “has deepened” even as the international environment has become more complex, said Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Friday (Nov 20).

Speaking at the start of a meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping, PM Wong said the two countries could build on their three government-to-government projects in China – a reference to the Suzhou Industrial Park, Sino-Singapore Tianjin-Eco City, and Chongqing Connectivity Initiative – to deepen their economic ties further.

“Singapore and China have achieved much together, and I look forward to discussing with President Xi how we can build on this very strong foundation and take our partnership further,” he said in his opening remarks.

The media were allowed to be in attendance only for the first few minutes of the leaders’ meeting at Kylin Villa, a sprawling state-owned lakeside resort nestled at the foot of Qilin Mountain and used for high-level official receptions. 

Xi said in Mandarin that cooperation over the past few years has brought tangible benefits to people in both countries.

“At present, the world is undergoing profound changes unseen in a century, with a new round of technological revolution and industrial transformation gaining momentum,” he added.

He described Singapore and China as friendly neighbours and key development partners, and called for closer strategic communication and cooperation to take their partnership to “new heights”.

“By doing so, we can better serve our respective modernisation efforts and make a positive contribution to regional and international prosperity and stability,” Xi said.

Kylin Villa was also where Xi hosted a historic summit with US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin on Thursday.  

“At a time of heightened geopolitical tensions, such dialogue is especially valuable as it contributes to greater understanding, peace, and stability for the entire world,” said PM Wong, who also congratulated Xi on China’s hosting of Apec and his meeting with Trump and Putin. 

Friday’s meeting was the third between PM Wong and Xi since PM Wong took office in May 2024. They last met in Beijing during PM Wong’s introductory visit in June 2025, following a first meeting on the sidelines of the Apec summit in Peru in November 2024.

PM Wong arrived in Shenzhen on Wednesday to attend the 33rd Apec Economic Leaders’ Meeting, shortly after the conclusion of the 49th Asean Summit in Manila, where Singapore formally assumed the bloc’s chairmanship.

At the Apec plenary session on Thursday, PM Wong urged leaders to keep Asia-Pacific from splitting into “competing economic blocs”.

He instead called for greater cooperation to “ensure that our region continues to be an engine of growth and prosperity for the world”.

Meanwhile, Xi said at the plenary that China will provide US$20 million to support “Apec’s practical cooperation”.  

PM Wong will next head to Beijing for a meeting and working lunch with Premier Li, before wrapping up his trip on Saturday.

data.title: Gold set for worst week since March on hawkish Fed, AI sell-off
data.description:
GOLD fell and was heading for the biggest weekly decline since March, as a hawkish Federal Reserve signalled more interest-rate hikes and a rout in artificial intelligence stocks pushed investors to sell the metal to cover losses.

Bullion dropped as much as 1.1 per cent on Friday (Nov 20) to below US$3,590 an ounce, and was on track to lose about 7 per cent in a week that has seen the metal slide to the lowest since September 2025.

Silver has fallen around 13 per cent in the same period. Fed Bank of Chicago president Austan Goolsbee on Thursday joined a number of central bank officials who have hinted at interest-rate hikes, saying he would consider all options to counter stubborn US inflation.

The prospect of tighter monetary policy kept US Treasury yields elevated, with 10-year borrowing costs poised to match a 2007 run of 29 closes above 5 per cent in the same year.

Globally, investors are betting that major central banks, including the Fed, European Central Bank and Bank of England, will keep rates largely unchanged for years once they have finished hiking at the end of 2027.

Higher interest rates and yields are typically negative for gold, which does not pay interest. A gauge of the US dollar has also risen 0.6 per cent this week, making bullion priced in the US currency more expensive for most buyers.

Gold is “now firmly in an air pocket, with very little technical support until the US$3,300 and US$3,400 region”, said Justin Lin, a strategist at Global X ETFs. The metal “looks very fragile now, and I struggle to see what could turn momentum around just yet”.

Bullion has fallen more than 30 per cent since the US-Iran war began in late February, as higher energy costs fuelled inflation.

The precious metal has also been caught up in a rout in technology stocks, with Asian equities tracking a decline on Wall Street driven by concerns around the AI trade.

Spot gold fell 0.8 per cent to US$3,596.09 an ounce at 9.01 am in Singapore.

Silver dropped 1.7 per cent to US$42.22 an ounce, after sinking nearly 5 per cent in the previous session. Platinum and palladium also declined. BLOOMBERG

data.title: What shattered Crystal Jade? How the culinary empire shrank from 120 to just 9 outlets
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] At its peak in 2015, Crystal Jade operated a sprawling global network of 120 restaurants, with 47 locations anchoring its presence in Singapore.

Today, the home-grown institution has retreated to just nine operating restaurants locally. Its central kitchen is shuttered and its holding companies are in receivership.

Last month, four outlets – three Crystal Jade La Mian Xiao Long Bao restaurants at Bugis Junction, Toa Payoh and i12 Katong, as well as Crystal Jade GO at Oasis Terraces in Punggol – ceased operations, retrenching around 120 workers.

What led to this dramatic contraction for a brand that used to witness long queues and once commanded a US$100 million private equity buyout? The Business Times traces Crystal Jade’s origins, what missteps may have led to its current distress and what is left in store for the brand.

Rise of the culinary empire

The origins of Crystal Jade date back to 1991, beginning as a singular Cantonese fine-dining restaurant in Singapore’s now-demolished Cairnhill Hotel. The venture initially struggled to gain traction, teetering on insolvency by its second year.

But its turning point came that same year, when Hong Kong-born entrepreneur Ip Yiu Tung injected S$2 million to secure a 49 per cent controlling stake in the ailing business.

Under Ip’s stewardship, the brand began a lucrative expansion into the mass-market segment with the launch of Crystal Jade Kitchen, moving away from a purely fine-dining Cantonese concept.

The new strategy transformed the once-struggling restaurant into a highly scalable holding company, generating an estimated S$240 million in annual turnover by 2009.

It soon attracted global institutional investors. In 2014, L Capital Asia (subsequently merged to form L Catterton) acquired a majority stake, valuing the enterprise at about US$100 million. L Capital Asia was a consumer PE firm set up in 2009 and sponsored by LVMH.

The complexity multiplier

Following the private equity buyout, the group’s portfolio was segmented into distinct categories: prestige fine dining anchored by concepts such as Crystal Jade Golden Palace, mid-tier casual dining such as Crystal Jade La Mian Xiao Long Bao, family-oriented Hong Kong Kitchen, and quick-service takeaway models under the CJ GO and My Bread banners.

While Crystal Jade is privately held, and neither its financial positions nor debt structure are publicly disclosed, some experts believe this expansion may have stretched Crystal Jade thin.

Geoffrey Tai, manager of lifestyle and consumer experience at Temasek Polytechnic, said that prior to L Capital Asia’s involvement, Crystal Jade originally had a clear structure.

Fine dining built its reputation, casual dining brought in customer volume, and its central kitchen helped maintain consistency while keeping costs under control, he said.

The aim was to aggressively replicate this operational density across multiple markets and dining tiers. But scaling the business became a “complexity multiplier”, Tai suggested.

“Expanding into fine dining, mid-tier casual and quick-service simultaneously across multiple geographies stretched management thin and forced the brand to compete in segments where its heritage equity bought it nothing,” he said.

Crystal Jade has the foundation of a strong brand reputation, but Tai emphasised that long-term success ultimately depends on understanding local consumers, maintaining a clear value proposition and adapting to market conditions.

“The real error was not deepening the moat in Singapore, where the brand was strongest, but spreading it thin across price tiers that cannibalised each other,” Tai added, noting the brand should have fortified its core competitive advantage rather than diluting it.

Geng Xuesong, associate professor of strategic management at Lee Kong Chian School of Business, Singapore Management University, said that there were strengths to the expansion strategy, but it was plausible that the operational complexity grew faster than the underlying restaurant unit economics and organisational capabilities.

“The managerial complexity would increase tremendously, particularly for new expansion like CJ GO, because its operations might require very different management and organisational capabilities from those Crystal Jade has built in other outlets,” he said.

Tai suggested that Crystal Jade’s portfolio was broad but not deep: premium outlets lacked exclusivity to command fine-dining margins, mid-tier outlets lacked differentiation, and quick-service outlets lacked the cost structure to win on price.

“In short, margin compression hit every tier at once,” he said.

L Catterton declined to comment on the strategy.

Squeezed middle

Simultaneously, the brand’s mid-tier segments found themselves caught in an increasingly polarised domestic dining scene.

“Premium dining thrives because they sell a special night out you can’t replicate at home, while casual dining thrives on pure speed and value. The middle is in trouble because it asks people to pay a 30 to 50 per cent premium over hawker food, without offering any of the ‘wow factor’ of fine dining,” Tai explained.

“Brands that are merely familiar, rather than distinctive, are particularly vulnerable,” Prof Geng said of the wider F&B field.

Sherri Kimes, an emeritus professor of operations management at Cornell University, said that midmarket restaurants can also struggle when their prices rise without a corresponding increase in perceived value.

“Whether that happened at Crystal Jade would require additional evidence,” she said.

Tai, on the other hand, was more convinced of the squeezed middle’s impact.

“In my view, that’s where Crystal Jade’s mid-tier got trapped – not cheap enough to compete on value, not unique enough to feel like a treat.

“Crystal Jade is just the most obvious example of what happens when a mid-tier Chinese restaurant gets stuck in no-man’s-land,” he said.

The crystal shatters

The company’s physical footprint began fracturing in 2026.

After quietly shuttering underperforming branches earlier in the year, the group contracted further in September and October, closing multiple mass-market and mid-tier outlets across Singapore and retrenching about 120 workers.

This was accompanied by the permanent closure of Crystal Jade Food Manufacturing, the group’s centralised kitchen.

Financial and risk advisory firm Kroll was appointed as receivers over Crystal Jade’s holding companies in Singapore and Hong Kong.

Keith Han, head of restructuring and insolvency at Bazul, explained that despite the receivership, the holding companies and the restaurants will continue to operate normally.

This legal move is understood as a way to facilitate L Catterton’s eventual exit from the brand. The private equity firm, Crystal Jade and Kroll declined to comment on the sale prospects.

Han noted that with the receivership in place, Kroll has the authority to sell off relevant assets to a prospective buyer without needing shareholder approval.

While details of the sale remain largely speculative, academics agreed that upon the sale, the incoming owner should execute some strategic pivots.

Prof Geng emphasised that the first priority should be to decide on the brand’s distinctive factor, rather than rely on the Crystal Jade name familiarity.

He noted his faith in its revival: “Crystal Jade is a valuable brand and heritage in Singapore, and it can be saved and revived if the new buyer can find out the sweet spot of how to utilise it in the right position and right portfolio.”

data.title: Same AI price, very different costs: What to automate in South-east Asia
data.description:
A CUSTOMER opens a chat to dispute a charge. Resolving it takes a staff member about 20 minutes.

In Singapore, that costs the company about US$7.90. In Indonesia, it costs about US$0.60.

Yet, a leading customer service software firm charges the same price in both markets for an artificial intelligence agent to handle that chat.

Board members across South-east Asia are now asking their executive teams which workflows to hand to AI agents.

Our answer is that the business case depends on where the work is done. We compare the cost of the staff who do the work today with the cost of the AI that would do it instead.

The cost of a workflow

We cover six markets: Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia. Our staff costs are based on official wage data for clerical or similar roles, and a 50 per cent addition for employer contributions, supervision and tools.

One customer service software firm charges from US$0.99 each time its AI agent resolves a chat. But AI agents may not be fully autonomous in customer service, so our calculations factor in human staff costs.

The same software firm reports that its AI agent resolves three chats in four on average. Results vary widely by business, so we assume a more cautious scenario, where the AI resolves six chats in 10. Staff still handle the other four.

The human part of the job then moves from routine handling to reviewing and deciding. The staff checks one in 10 chats, taking three minutes each time.

For a business handling 20,000 chats a month, we assume half a full-time employee is required just to manage and maintain the agent.

By our calculations, at US$0.99 per outcome and even after a business pays for the staff it still needs, an AI agent cuts the cost of a chat in Singapore by about half.

In Malaysia, it cuts the cost by about a quarter, and in Thailand by about a tenth. In Vietnam, it saves nothing. In the Philippines and Indonesia, it adds to the cost.

These figures are illustrative estimates based on a single workflow and average wages, which mask wide variances between firms. In reality too, large clients often negotiate published prices down.

Our calculation also excludes the cost of building an agent, connecting it to existing systems and keeping it up to date as models change.

Businesses must therefore run the maths using their own data.

The success rate matters too. If the agent resolves only half of all chats, the savings in Singapore fall to about 40 per cent. If the agent resolves three in four, the savings rise to about 60 per cent. Singapore still saves the most and Indonesia still loses the most.

The reference firm charges for each chat its agent resolves. In higher-wage markets where staff cost more than about US$1 a chat, an agent with a higher resolution rate saves more money.

But where staff costs less, as in the Philippines and Indonesia, every extra chat the agent resolves actually adds to the cost.

The “build vs buy” variable

Some firms build their own agents rather than buy one from a vendor. For them, the choice of AI model matters a great deal.

For this scenario, we estimated costs for six leading models, based on their published prices. (Models we studied were Claude Sonnet 5.5, GPT-6 Astra, Gemini 3.8 Flash, GLM-5.2, DeepSeek-V4-Flash and Qwen 3.5.)

With the cheapest model, the self-built AI agent costs less than staff in every market. With the most expensive, it costs more everywhere except Singapore.

Engineering also makes a difference. When building an agent, design can directly affect the bottom line.

Take a mid-priced model: An agent that wastefully rereads twice as much company material at every step would lose its savings in Thailand, Vietnam, the Philippines and Indonesia.

An agent engineered to cache material, instead of rereading it, would pay off in all six markets.

Does running AI locally shift the case?

Today, most AI models run in a few giant data centres, mostly outside South-east Asia, and are sold at one global price.

As more countries insist on data sovereignty, keeping data and AI processing at home, more AI is likely to run locally. It would then carry local costs, including power and the cost of meeting each country’s rules and regulations.

Power is the easiest of these costs to measure. Electricity for a data centre costs about three times as much in Singapore as in Indonesia. Still, that makes the same AI only about 10 per cent more expensive.

By contrast, staff costs nearly 13 times as much. So even if AI runs locally, wages are likely to decide where AI agents make commercial sense. The cost of compliance is the open question.

Moving prices and looking beyond costs

Leading AI companies currently spend far more than they earn.

OpenAI expects to burn through about US$280 billion between 2026 and 2030, according to company projections reported by the Financial Times.

Prices may therefore rise. On our estimates, if a mid-priced model trebled its token prices, the savings from AI would disappear everywhere in South-east Asia except Singapore.

Exchange rates add a second risk. AI prices are set in US dollars.

A weaker ringgit, baht, dong or rupiah makes the AI agent more expensive in local terms, while local salaries stay roughly the same.

Still, costs may not be the only consideration. AI agents work around the clock; they can absorb sudden peaks in demand, help launch new services faster and create new ways to serve customers.

Where an AI agent saves little in operating costs, these benefits could still justify deploying one.

What leaders should do

Start with the process. Map each workflow and remove unnecessary steps. Every step an AI agent performs adds cost.

Then ask three simple questions of each workflow: One, what does it cost us today? Two, what will it cost with an AI agent, including the staff it still needs? Three, how far could AI prices rise, or the local currency fall, before the business case fails?

Answer these questions separately for each market. Where the savings are small or negative, name the other benefits you expect in advance and measure them.

Crucially, businesses should keep the decision reversible for as long as possible.

Once teams are reshaped around AI agents, the know-how to do the work without them may be lost, and rebuilding that is slow and costly.

A phased roll-out is sensible. Each phase shows what the agent can handle before more of the workflow depends on it.

Avoid tying the workflow to a single provider or model. If that provider changes its terms, retires a model or fails, the business should be able to switch without starting over.

AI may cost the same in every market, but the case for it is won or lost, workflow by workflow and market by market.

Daniel Liebau is an adjunct associate professor with the Asian Institute of Digital Finance at the National University of Singapore, and the founding managing director of Lightbulb Capital, an innovation advisory firm. Damien Kopp is the founder and managing director of RebootUp, an AI advisory firm, and associate faculty, executive development, at Singapore Management University.

Workings are available from the authors on request.

data.title: Stocks to watch: Yangzijiang Shipbuilding, Seatrium, Frencken
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] The following companies saw new developments that may affect trading of their securities on Thursday (Nov 19):

Yangzijiang Shipbuilding : The shipbuilder’s subsidiary has entered into an investment agreement with China’s Taicang Port Economic and Technological Development Zone. The agreement is in relation to a project to develop a clean energy vessel intelligent manufacturing base in Taicang city, located in Jaingsu province. The group expects capital expenditure for the project to be about 3.38 billion yuan (US$507 million). Shares of Yangzijiang Shipbuilding ended 1.6 per cent or S$0.07 higher at S$4.39 on Wednesday, before the announcement.

Seatrium : The offshore, marine and energy specialist reported that its net order book stood at S$12.2 billion as at end-September, comprising 35 projects with deliveries extending through 2033. It had secured S$1.7 billion in new orders so far this year. Seatrium expects its underlying net profit for FY2026 to be materially higher than in FY2025. The counter ended 0.6 per cent or S$0.01 lower at S$1.71, before the news.

Frencken : The technology manufacturer announced on Wednesday (Nov 18) a 31.3 per cent year-on-year increase in earnings to S$13 million for its third quarter ended Sep 30. Revenue grew 12.8 per cent to S$238.5 million, from S$211.5 million a year earlier. The increase was mainly driven by Frencken’s mechatronics division’s revenue, which rose 13.4 per cent to S$214.3 million. The counter ended S$0.01, or 0.6 per cent, up at S$1.71 before the news.

data.title: âChilling effectâ: US chips curb could slow down Asean data centre expansion, Malaysia and Thailand at higher risk, say analysts
data.description:
[SINGAPORE] Washington’s new curbs on advanced artificial intelligence chips could slow down the next phase of growth for South-east Asia’s data centre build-out, analysts said.

Malaysia and Thailand face greater risks from the restrictions due to their exposure to non-US data centre customers, while Singapore could see delays to its next wave of data centre development, they added.

The rule, issued by the US Department of Commerce on Monday (Nov 16), requires licences for advanced AI chips shipped to Singapore, Malaysia, Indonesia, Thailand and Brazil, with exemptions for US-headquartered companies.

The five countries account for about 7 to 9 per cent of the world’s operational data centre capacity at about 5.5 gigawatt (GW) of IT load, noted a DBS Group Research note released on Tuesday.

CGS International (CGSI) expects the ruling to benefit US hyperscalers, while DBS also noted that the rule could shift AI infrastructure investment “towards jurisdictions and operators facing fewer regulatory hurdles”.

“China-facing AI projects and independent graphics processing unit (GPU)-cloud operators face higher execution risks,” it noted in a report.

Malaysia and Thailand face greater exposure risk

Over in Malaysia, of the 8.4 GW of data centre power supply agreements signed with the government as at June, about 30 per cent is linked to US-headquartered companies.

The remaining users are “less clear”, noted the research house.

Meanwhile, colocation demand in Thailand data centres is also expected to slow down as the data centre operators that serve Chinese tech companies have to obtain US export licences when importing advanced AI chips from the US.

In Singapore, CGSI analysts said it believes the build-out for the second Data Centre Call for Application (DC-CFA2) and the upcoming data-centre park in Jurong Island “could be deferred”.

The research house cited “the potential souring of sentiments and demand”, following the new US rule as the primary reason for the slowdown.

In Singapore, four data centre operators – Digital Realty, Equinix, STT GDC and Keppel – were each provisionally allocated 50 megawatts (MW) under the DC-CFA2 tender in August.

Cristina Brayton-Lewis, partner at law firm White & Case, expects some “chilling effect” on data centre operators in Asean.

As a result of the new rule, some projects “may not be able to obtain necessary licences”, she said. “Other projects may be able to secure licences, but may face delays in licensing or potentially burdensome licensing conditions.”

Foo Zhiwei, analyst at Macquarie Capital, expects a “slowdown, not a halt”, as operators deal with the extra licensing requirements and additional know-your-customer checks.

DBS Group Research noted that the licensing requirements could delay GPU shipments and AI deployments.

The effects will be felt most among non-US cloud operators, noted DBS.

Operators still report strong demand

Serene Nah, managing director and head of Asia-Pacific at Digital Realty, said that the operator is still choosing tenants for its upcoming SIN13 data centre facility.

“We’re approached by so many people because we have the 50 MW, so we have to pick,” she said.

She added that the SIN13 data centre will host mostly AI inference and high-performance computing. Therefore, the company may lean towards companies that can more easily import GPUs under the new rules.

That said, she noted that the new rules means that the operator will “need to be more selective” of the customers it selects for the data centre.

Keppel, another of the four awarded capacity through the DC-CFA2, said it does not expect the measures to have a significant impact on its data centre business in Singapore.

“Most of our Singapore data centres, including the floating data centre under construction, are predominantly committed to US-based hyperscalers,” said a Keppel spokesperson.

Despite the restrictions, CGSI expects an upside for Singapore operators.

“(Singapore) could benefit over time if it establishes itself as a trusted computing hub for compliant workloads and hyperscalers,” the research house noted.

Chip suppliers at risk

While demand for operators remains strong, analysts warned that chip suppliers are at the biggest risk.

AEM is directly exposed through its AI and high-performance computing customers, while UMS, Frencken and Venture could be impacted indirectly, noted CGSI.

“We think the key risk to earnings is a slower and more measured demand pace from customers, which could potentially affect earnings growth pace over FY2027 and (potentially) FY2028,” noted the research house.

However, DBS said that the impact on equipment makers is limited.

“The measures primarily target advanced computing chips rather than equipment,” said DBS, noting that UMS and Frencken are less affected.

“While slower AI capacity expansion could eventually weigh on wafer fab equipment spending, UMS and Frencken are less affected in the near term.”

However, DBS noted that Venture might be affected, given its exposure to AI infrastructure hardware, networking and test equipments

Overall, CGSI expects investments to slow down mainly “as investors await licensing clarity”.

Prime Minister Lawrence Wong on Tuesday said Singapore can facilitate US checks on companies and how advanced chips brought into the country are deployed, if Washington has concerns.

He noted that a large portion of chips recorded, as sales to Singapore never enter the country.

“Only a small volume of those chips’ directly comes into Singapore,” said PM Wong.

data.title: When AI systems are compromised, detection without recovery is not resilience
data.description:
RECENT data breaches involving MoneySmart, M1 and Doctor Anywhere have put cyber risks back in focus for Singapore businesses.

On Nov 13, the Cyber Security Agency of Singapore urged all organisations to “take immediate steps to strengthen their cyberdefences”.

While most conversations have focused on how these incidents happened and what information was exposed, they raise a bigger, more urgent question for business leaders. If critical systems are hit, how long can the business afford to be out of action before the financial, operational and reputational damage begin to pile up?

Consider two incidents with very different outcomes.

In September 2026, Boustead Singapore disclosed that an overseas business unit had isolated affected systems, activated business continuity procedures and recovered critical data and systems from backups following a cyberincident. Its operations suffered no material disruption.

Contrast that with the 2025 cyberattack on Marks & Spencer, which forced systems offline and disrupted online operations for weeks.

While physical stores continued trading, customers could not access certain online shopping services, with operations returning in phases.

The circumstances were different, but both incidents highlight a key point. Getting systems back online is one thing; knowing whether the business can safely resume operations is another.

As organisations give artificial-intelligence agents access to sensitive systems, leaders must ask: Can the team determine what happened, contain the consequences and safely reverse unintended outcomes?

Commvault’s 2026 State of Data Resilience report found that only 45 per cent of organisations in Singapore are very confident that they could identify a compromised AI system.

If organisations are not even confident they can identify a compromised AI system, determining what has been affected, what needs to be recovered, and whether the team can restore it to a clean, trusted state could be even more challenging.

AI changes the nature of the blast radius

As AI moves from assisting employees to acting on their behalf, the nature of operational risk changes.

An autonomous AI agent may make decisions and take actions across multiple connected systems using identities and permissions legitimately granted by the organisation.

This autonomy creates business value, but it also means that a compromised identity, inaccurate data, incomplete instruction or poorly designed workflow can trigger consequences across data, applications and business processes before a person has time to intervene.

The challenge then is to understand the chain of actions that followed.

What data did the system access? What decisions did it influence? Which transactions did it initiate? What downstream processes accepted its output? Which actions need to be reversed, reconciled or reviewed. Without that understanding, an organisation cannot know whether the incident is truly contained.

And if it cannot establish which data and systems remain trustworthy, restoring the affected technology may not be enough.

Recover what the business needs, then prove that it works

No organisation can restore everything at once. Recovery, therefore, needs to begin with understanding which capabilities the business needs first, and what those capabilities depend on.

The minimum viable company, or MVC, defines the systems, data and operations that must remain available, or be restored first, for the organisation to continue functioning during disruption.

An MVC differs by organisation. For a bank, it might include enabling customers to make time-critical payments and withdraw funds.

For a logistics provider, it might mean accepting shipping instructions, tracking goods in transit and releasing deliveries at their destination.

The priority is to determine which business processes must continue or be restored first, and then map the systems, data, people and other dependencies needed to support them.

The same principle applies to AI. One business process supported by AI may require rapid recovery, while another one may tolerate a longer interruption.

Prioritisation should therefore be based on business impact and recovery requirements, not simply on whether a workload uses AI.

It must also account for the identities, applications, infrastructure and data required to restore the complete business process safely.

Boards do not need to know every recovery dependency or direct the operational response.

But they should require evidence that management has identified the organisation’s critical business capabilities, and agreed on the order in which they will be restored cleanly and tested so that they can operate safely following disruption.

The next test for trusted AI: Recovery readiness

As Singapore advances trusted AI, resilience must become part of that trust. Guardrails matter, but so does knowing the business can recover when those are not enough.

As AI moves from assisting to acting, recovery readiness must become part of AI readiness.

Singapore businesses must be able to demonstrate that they can contain unintended consequences, restore critical operations and recover safely when existing safeguards fall short.

The writer is field chief technology officer for Asia-Pacific at Commvault

AI tools were used to support research, framework development and proofreading of the article before submission
